title: 5.9.4 Challenges: Polish it your way
description: Your table works and feels better already. Add one more polish of your own: popups that fade instead of vanishing, a tilt rule that punishes shaking the table, or a heavier ball from round 2. Pick one; add an idea of your own on top if you like.

steps.title: Pick a polish and add it
hints: Whatever you pick, press R afterwards and check the game still starts cleanly.
Challenge 2: the push lines can sit inside if (!tilted) { ... } so a tilted table stops nudging too.

steps.title: Name what you polished
steps.instructions: At the top of `script.js`, write one sentence as a `//` comment saying what your polish is and what a player would notice without it.
hints: 'Popups fade, so a hit looks smooth' names a polish. 'I changed some code' does not.

requirements.title: Your polish is in the code
requirements.description: Any one challenge counts: a popup that fades through .opacity, a tilt rule (a count of nudges that goes up or a budget that counts down, a frameCount window, or more than 3 nudges), a ball whose mass changes from round 2 (set inside an if, from a variable, or in a helper of its own), or a polish of your own that changes play: a score multiplier or bonus, or gravityScale, rotationLock, bounciness or friction moved off its starting value. Help: 5.7.1 (Reading: Words on a sprite, and sprites that run out) and 5.8.1 (Reading: Four knobs: mass, gravityScale, rotationLock, debug)
requirements.hint: Pick one challenge from step 1 and add its lines: a fade, a tilt count, or a heavier ball from round 2.

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote a moSHion sketch (p5-style JavaScript with a physics world) for the lab "5.9.4 Challenges: Polish it your way". The task they were given: The pinball table is finished (labelled bumpers, popups with .life, a chime, a held-key nudge with applyForce, a ball mass and debug). Add one polish: (1) popups that fade: keep each popup in a list and lower its .opacity every frame, for example p.opacity = p.life / 40; (2) a tilt rule: count nudges (add 1 on each kb.presses of an arrow), reset the count every 120 frames with frameCount % 120 === 0, and when the count goes above 3 lose the ball (for example ball.y = 500) and show TILT until R, which resets the count; or (3) a heavier ball in round 2: a round counter (the step calls it roundNumber, because round is already moSHion's round() function) that goes up on R, and a bigger .mass from round 2 on, with the round shown on screen. One of the three is enough, and an idea of the student's own on top is welcome. Step 2 also asks for a one-sentence // comment at the top naming the polish; no criterion checks that comment. What the starter file already had: everything from 5.8.3, including ball.mass set once in setup(), so that line alone is not a new polish. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do when the sketch runs. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, if / else chains or ternaries, helper functions, template strings, arrow functions, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine, and so is moving the rules into update(). Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment or inside a string never runs, so a line the student only wrote in a comment does not count, and the starter's STEP comments are never the student's work. moSHion facts that matter here: .opacity runs from 1 (solid) to 0 (invisible) and fades the sprite's colour and words together; a fourth number in fill() is ignored by moSHion. .life counts down one per frame, so .life / 40 slides from 1 to 0 for a popup made with .life = 40. A deleted sprite stays in an array but is no longer drawn. frameCount % 120 === 0 is true on every 120th frame. kb.presses is true on the one frame a key goes down. Read the whole sketch and look for any one of the three, written any way, or a polish of the student's own that changes how the game plays or reads (for example a gravityScale, rotationLock, bounciness or friction change, a timer, a countdown, a score multiplier or bonus). A change only to a colour or a fixed size is not a polish. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise. Write for a 14-year-old reader: short sentences and plain, everyday words.

rubric.title: Your polish is in the code
rubric.description: At least one of: (1) popups whose .opacity goes down over time (worked out from .life, lowered by a step each frame, or similar); (2) a tilt rule: a count of nudges that goes up on a key press, reset on a frameCount beat or by R, and something that happens when it goes above 3; (3) a ball whose mass grows from round 2 (a round counter that R raises, and a mass set from it or inside an if on it); or a polish of the student's own that changes play, such as a score multiplier or bonus, or a gravityScale, rotationLock, bounciness or friction change. Missing: none of these, or only a colour or a fixed size changed. Help: 5.7.1 (Reading: Words on a sprite, and sprites that run out) and 5.8.1 (Reading: Four knobs: mass, gravityScale, rotationLock, debug)
